sprinkler-run-time-calculator.title: The catch-cup test
sprinkler-run-time-calculator.alt: Diagram of a catch-cup test: six cans spread across a lawn zone, run for 15 minutes, then the average depth multiplied by 4 gives inches per hour.
sprinkler-run-time-calculator.caption: Run one zone for 15 minutes, average the water in the cups, and multiply by 4 to get your sprinkler's rate in inches per hour.

lawn-fertilizer-calculator.title: Reading the bag
lawn-fertilizer-calculator.alt: Diagram of a fertilizer bag labelled 32-0-4 showing nitrogen, phosphate and potash percentages, and the sum 1 pound of nitrogen divided by 0.32 equals 3.1 pounds of product per 1,000 square feet.
lawn-fertilizer-calculator.caption: The first number is the nitrogen percentage. To apply 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft from a 32-0-4 product, spread 1 ÷ 0.32 ≈ 3.1 lb.

lawn-lime-calculator.title: Where your soil pH sits
lawn-lime-calculator.alt: A soil pH scale from 4 to 9 with the 5.5 to 7.0 target range for lawns highlighted; lime raises low pH and sulfur lowers high pH.
lawn-lime-calculator.caption: Lawns and vegetable gardens do best around pH 5.5–7.0 (University of Maryland Extension). Lime raises pH; sulfur lowers it. Your soil test tells you how much.

square-foot-garden-planner.title: One square, 1 to 16 plants
square-foot-garden-planner.alt: A 4 by 4 foot raised bed divided into 16 one-foot squares, with examples of 1, 4, 9 and 16 plants per square.
square-foot-garden-planner.caption: Each 1-foot square holds 1, 4, 9 or 16 plants depending on plant size: one tomato, four lettuces, nine bush beans or sixteen carrots.

raised-bed-soil-calculator.title: Measure the bed, fill the volume
raised-bed-soil-calculator.alt: Cut-away raised bed 8 feet long, 4 feet wide and 1 foot deep, filled with a soil and compost mix, totalling 32 cubic feet or about 1.2 cubic yards.
raised-bed-soil-calculator.caption: Length × width × depth gives cubic feet; divide by 27 for cubic yards. An 8 × 4 ft bed filled 12 in deep holds 32 cu ft, about 1.2 cu yd.

mulch-calculator.title: 2 to 3 inches, flat and wide
mulch-calculator.alt: Cross-section of a garden bed with a 2 to 3 inch layer of mulch over the soil and a bare gap left around the base of a shrub.
mulch-calculator.caption: Spread mulch 2 to 3 inches deep in an even layer, and keep it an inch or two back from stems and trunks.

compost-calculator.title: How deep to spread compost
compost-calculator.alt: Three cross-sections comparing compost depths: 3 to 4 inches mixed into a new bed, 1/4 to 1 inch as a yearly top-up, and about 1/4 inch as lawn topdressing.
compost-calculator.caption: Depths from Oregon State University Extension: 3–4 in mixed into new beds, ¼–1 in a year as a top-up, about ¼ in as lawn topdressing.

sod-calculator.title: Lay sod like bricks
sod-calculator.alt: Top view of sod slabs laid in rows with the joints staggered like brickwork, starting along a straight edge, with measurements for a rectangular lawn area.
sod-calculator.caption: Measure the area, add a few percent for cuts, and lay the slabs in staggered rows starting from a straight edge such as a driveway.

grass-seed-calculator.title: New lawn or overseeding?
grass-seed-calculator.alt: Side-by-side lawn plots: bare soil seeded at the full new-lawn rate on the left, and a thin existing lawn overseeded at a lower rate on the right.
grass-seed-calculator.caption: A bare-soil lawn needs the full seeding rate for your grass type; overseeding a thin lawn uses a lower rate because grass is already there.

gravel-calculator.title: Area × depth = stone to order
gravel-calculator.alt: Cross-section of a gravel path showing 3 inches of crushed stone over firm soil, with the formula area times depth divided by 12 for cubic feet, divided by 27 for cubic yards, times about 1.4 for tons.
gravel-calculator.caption: A 30 × 3 ft path at 3 in deep needs about 0.88 cubic yards, roughly 1.2 tons of crushed stone at 1.4 tons per yard.

topsoil-calculator.title: Filling low spots and new beds
topsoil-calculator.alt: Cross-section of uneven lawn ground with a low spot filled with topsoil to level, and a new lawn area with 4 to 6 inches of topsoil spread over subsoil.
topsoil-calculator.caption: Measure how deep each low spot is, or use 4–6 in of good topsoil when preparing ground for seed. One cubic yard covers about 81 sq ft at 4 in.

paver-base-calculator.title: Layers under a paver patio
paver-base-calculator.alt: Cross-section of a paver patio: pavers on 1 inch of bedding sand over 4 to 6 inches of compacted base, with the base extending past the paver edge by the same distance as its depth.
paver-base-calculator.caption: Unilock's guideline for patios and walkways: 4–6 in of compacted base, about 1 in of bedding sand, and a base that extends past the edge as far as it is deep.

when-to-fertilize-lawn.title: When to feed your lawn
when-to-fertilize-lawn.alt: Calendar chart: cool-season lawns get their main feeding in late summer to early fall and a second in late spring; warm-season lawns are fed from late spring through summer after green-up.
when-to-fertilize-lawn.caption: Cool-season grass: main feeding late summer to early fall, a lighter one in late spring. Warm-season grass: feed after green-up through summer, and stop in late summer.

how-to-water-new-grass-seed.title: Watering new seed, stage by stage
how-to-water-new-grass-seed.alt: Three stages of watering new grass seed: light watering about twice a day until germination, then less often but deeper once seedlings are 1 to 2 inches, then about once a week after two or three mowings.
how-to-water-new-grass-seed.caption: Keep the surface moist until germination (2–3 weeks), water less often but deeper once seedlings reach 1–2 in, then switch to about once a week after two or three mowings.

fall-lawn-care-checklist.title: Fall lawn care, in order
fall-lawn-care-checklist.alt: Fall lawn care timeline for cool-season lawns: seed and core aerate from late August to mid-September; fertilize and soil test in mid-September; treat broadleaf weeds, keep mowing, deal with leaves and water in dry spells into early November; then a last mow and winter storage before the ground freezes.
fall-lawn-care-checklist.caption: For cool-season lawns: seed and aerate late August to mid-September, feed in mid-September, keep mowing and managing leaves into November, and put tools away before the ground freezes.

how-to-read-soil-test.title: Reading a soil test report
how-to-read-soil-test.alt: Simplified soil test report showing pH, buffer pH, phosphorus, potassium, organic matter and CEC, with notes explaining what each result means.
how-to-read-soil-test.caption: The key lines: pH (5.5–7.0 is the usual lawn and vegetable target), buffer pH for lime needs, phosphorus and potassium levels, organic matter and CEC.

how-to-overseed-lawn.title: Overseeding in seven steps
how-to-overseed-lawn.alt: Seven-step overseeding sequence: find why the lawn is thin, pick the right time, mow short and clear debris, open up the soil, spread seed, water lightly and often, care for the new grass.
how-to-overseed-lawn.caption: The order matters: fix the cause, seed at the right time, mow short, loosen the soil so seed touches it, then keep it moist until it is established.

how-to-lay-sod.title: Laying sod the right way
how-to-lay-sod.alt: Steps for laying sod: start along a straight edge, stagger the joints like bricks, butt the edges tight without overlapping, cut pieces to fit curves, roll lightly and water right away.
how-to-lay-sod.caption: Start along a straight edge, stagger joints like brickwork, butt edges tight without stretching, roll lightly, then water thoroughly right away.

raised-bed-soil-mixes.title: Three raised bed soil mixes
raised-bed-soil-mixes.alt: Comparison of three raised bed fills: a 50/50 mix of topsoil and compost, the square foot gardening mix of one-third compost, one-third peat or coir and one-third vermiculite, and a bagged raised bed mix.
raised-bed-soil-mixes.caption: Topsoil and compost 50/50 is cheapest in bulk; the square foot gardening mix (⅓ compost, ⅓ peat or coir, ⅓ vermiculite) is lightest; bagged mixes are easiest for small beds.

mulching-mistakes.title: Mulch volcano vs. mulch doughnut
mulching-mistakes.alt: Side-by-side comparison: wrong, mulch piled high against a tree trunk in a volcano; right, a wide flat ring of mulch 2 to 3 inches deep with a bare circle around the trunk.
mulching-mistakes.caption: Don't pile mulch against the trunk. Spread a wide, flat ring 2–3 inches deep and leave a bare circle a few inches across around the trunk.

how-much-water-does-lawn-need.title: About an inch a week, rain included
how-much-water-does-lawn-need.alt: A weekly water budget for a cool-season lawn: about 1 inch total per week, with an example of 0.5 inch from rain and 0.5 inch from the sprinklers, watered deeply once or twice.
how-much-water-does-lawn-need.caption: Cool-season lawns need about 1–1½ inches of water a week (University of Illinois Extension), and rain counts. Water deeply and infrequently to make up the difference.

spring-lawn-care-checklist.title: Spring lawn care, in order
spring-lawn-care-checklist.alt: Spring lawn care timeline: in early spring rake, get the mower ready and test the soil; in mid-spring when forsythia blooms apply crabgrass preventer if needed and seed bare spots early; in late spring mow high, fertilize and check the sprinklers.
spring-lawn-care-checklist.caption: Early spring: clean up, ready the mower and test the soil. When forsythia blooms: crabgrass preventer if needed. Late spring: mow high, fertilize and check your sprinklers.

how-to-build-gravel-path.title: Building a gravel path
how-to-build-gravel-path.alt: Cross-section of a gravel path: a trench about 4 inches deep, edging on both sides, about 2.5 inches of compacted base stone, landscape fabric, then surface gravel filled to about half an inch below the top of the edging.
how-to-build-gravel-path.caption: This Old House's method: dig about 4 in, set edging, tamp about 2½ in of base stone, lay landscape fabric, then fill surface gravel to about ½ in below the edging.

how-to-level-bumpy-lawn.title: Two ways to level a lawn
how-to-level-bumpy-lawn.alt: Two methods: for shallow dips, topdress with up to half an inch of leveling mix at a time and let the grass grow through; for dips deeper than about an inch, cut and lift the sod, fill underneath with soil, and lay it back.
how-to-level-bumpy-lawn.caption: Shallow dips: topdress no more than ½ in at a time and let the grass grow through before repeating. Dips deeper than about 1 in: lift the sod, fill beneath it, and relay it.
